statement: King Njoya of the Bamum Kingdom (Cameroon) invented the Bamum script starting 1896, evolving through six documented stages over c. 14 years (1896-1910): from an initial 465-pictogram/10-digit system ("Lewa") through intermediate forms to a true syllabary by 1902 onward. Used for a pharmacopoeia, a calendar, legal/administrative records, schools, a library, and a printing press. Suppressed after French colonial administration took over in 1919 (materials destroyed, teaching banned); undergoing a documented revival since 2022 via the Endangered Alphabets Project working with Njoya's great-grandson.

sources.citation: africanhistoryextra.com, "The invention of writing in an African kingdom."
